question.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y+1}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y+1}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{e}^{y+1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,$ $\text{d}u=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  & =2{\int }_{1}^{3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{e}^{u}{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =2{e}^{3}-2e \\  & =2e({e}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$
